The decay time of the $B^0_s$ meson from the Bbar $^0_s$ and $B^0_s$ states is studied, specifically their average decay times and the difference between them. LHCb uses a specialized likelihood method to separate these lifetimes by analyzing $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays with two trusted flavor tags, accounting for any detection biases. The measured average decay times are found to be 0.482±± 12 ps for Bbar $^0_s$ and 0.479±± 11 ps for $B^0_s$. The corresponding tagged differences are generally within the expected error margins. Integrating the tagged results with less certain measurements of the time distribution's asymmetry yields a combined average decay time of 0.470± 0 24 ps for Bbar $^0_s$ and 0 4 6 8 ± 0 2 6 ± 0 2 8 ps for $B^0_s$.

This research paper focuses on the discrete distributed regulation issue in a stochastic parabolic equation, where the control and source terms are randomly affected. The state and control variables have a specific relationship to their spatial dimensions. To tackle this challenge, a finite element method is applied to approximate the solution, with particular attention paid to achieving optimal convergence rates. The related deterministic case is also examined.

The highest-energy particles reaching Earth from space, called cosmic rays, show significant variations in direction as they approach our planet. Measuring these direction-based variations above 4 EeV energy levels is especially challenging due to limited observational data at the edges of the observatory's path. To overcome this challenge, researchers employed an advanced statistical method that accounts for anisotropy in three dimensions and across different energy levels. By utilizing nearly 10 years of data collected by the Pierre Auger Observatory, a more sensitive method was used to identify an anisotropy in the arrival directions of cosmic rays. An anisotropy in the form of a wave with two parts was found in different energy levels, with an anisotropy in the form of a harmonic in the northwestern part of the sky appearing in opposite directions and with greater significance. With over 3 standard deviations of confidence, this discovery suggests a possible influence from magnetic fields in our galaxy on the highest-energy particles from space.

The ATLAS detector at the LHC gathered p+Pb data with a center of mass energy of 5.02 TeV at the end of 2018, enabling an almost complete coverage of charged particle moments, including those derived from dN/deta, dN/dphi, and two-particle correlations, as well as a variety of nuclear modification factors, including central-to-peripheral ratios, for a wide range of collision centralities. This study builds upon earlier analyses by extending the dataset and incorporating new studies, providing a comprehensive overview of charged particle behavior under various conditions. Notably, nch has been updated to 1.42, supporting recent recalculations of the ATLAS Pb beam noise threshold in the search for scalar dark matter production. Furthermore, RpPb 0.34 has been revised to a revised value of 0.34, offering a refined benchmark for fundamental research into the formation and evolution of nuclear matter formed in p+Pb collisions and QCD calculations.

A general class of noncommutative harmonic oscillators has been investigated in this study, where the noncommutativity parameter $\theta$ influences the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$.  The effects of noncommutativity on the system's properties, including its harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian, path integrals, and both noncommutative and commutative scattering probabilities, are derived here.  Additionally, a comparison with their conventional commutative counterparts is provided.

In evaluating the responses of Immunotherapies, a method is categorized into five distinct groups based on the presence of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes within a pathology report. A challenging classification problem, this method relies on text reports that can vary in style and is subjected to federal learning principles. In this framework, a centrally coordinated server initiates the process by creating a foundational model and sharing it with participating institutions. These entities utilize their own patient data to refine their respective models without exchanging information among them. Following a series of local training iterations, updated model updates are collectively used to enhance the foundational model in a coordinated manner. This process is repeated until the desired performance is achieved. A real-world application involving 26 Italian hospitals demonstrated the technique's potential in categorizing patient responses to a specific immunotherapy treatment, alongside an in-depth analysis of the features contributing to the fifth pathology group defined by the Hamacher et al. method. Two additional approaches were also tested to compare the results.

In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, operating at 100 Gbit/s using the decision feedback equalizer (DFE) as a method to equalize chromatic dispersion in a sea test span of 39.8 nsec of submarine fiber. Although the DFE effectively compensates for inter-symbol interference caused by chromatic dispersion, its performance suffers from incorrect feedback clicks leading to error propagation. To mitigate this issue, a novel equalization scheme is developed, which incorporates a enhanced electrical Hilbert transform into the DFE structure. This new method allows for more accurate click identification and was successfully tested in the field trial, where it showed significant improvement in reducing error propagation with Feff dh as a result. Specifically, the enhanced DFE with H-DFE exhibited a substantial decrease in the error propagation coefficient compared to its counterpart, which led to a greater margin between the actual received power and the required power for a given bit error rate after forward error correction, particularly in high-velocity scenarios where the Brinkman number (Bn) exceeds a certain threshold.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have demonstrated superior performance and efficiency in various computer vision tasks, but their substantial number of parameters can hinder real-time operation. To address this issue, researchers developed Temporal DCNNs (TDCNNs) by integrating Tensor Operations into RNNs. While TDCNNs have improved training speed and flexibility, they still suffer from excessive parameters. In response, we introduce a new network structure optimization method called Pruning In Time (PIT), which selectively removes redundant parameters during training. By identifying and eliminating unnecessary parameters, PIT enables more flexible and efficient model training. Our experiments show that PIT-out performs better than conventional DCNNs and PR-DCNNs in multiple tasks, including Scene Classification, Emotion Recognition and Video Classification.

It has been proven that every Zinbiel algebra possessing a direct summing property is solvable, which means that its lower central series eventually results in the zero ideal. Furthermore, it has been shown that all simple Zinbiel algebras are direct sums of indecomposable algebras.

This study explores one method for investigating long-term fluctuations in Pb-Pb collisions at a high energy level of 5.02 TeV, which can offer insights into event-by-event variations in flow angle. We have employed a specific analytical approach using two-dimensional spectral density functions to estimate the standard deviation of flow angle spectra in various quick-measurement intervals. By simulating data with known fluctuations in the simulation, we verified that our approach can effectively identify these variations. Furthermore, our study found that certain quick-measurement interval ratios are capable of detecting simulated fluctuations of flow magnitude and angle with a high level of accuracy. These findings suggest that our approach has the potential to be utilized in experimental settings to investigate the fluctuations in magnitude and angle of flow in high-energy collisions.

This paper stands as the first instance of the integrated inverse semigroup theory within the equational basis of DLE-logics, specifically DLE-polynomials. We have derived a formula for the inverse of a polynomial with multiple variables, and this particular equation is referred to as the unified inverse relation. The proof of the relation is also provided for all DLE-algebras with a specified arity.

Inaccurate or conflicting data entries are a prevalent issue in databases, impacting systems that rely on data tables for operation. These problems, known as inconsistencies, can arise from faulty data input, system errors, or the integration of disparate databases. The concept of functional dependencies is frequently employed to identify relationships between data columns, typically seen in forms like "one person has a single social security number." This study explores the application of functional dependencies to identify and address inconsistencies, focusing on methods to handle missing data (referred to as nulls). The research presents a comprehensive framework called $\mathcal{F}\!\!\mathcal{O}\!\!\mathcal{C}\!\!\mathcal{U}\!\!\mathcal{S}$, which serves to represent and analyze tables containing missing entries along with functional dependencies. The framework enables the detection of violations, visualizes inconsistency patterns, and facilitates the identification of conflicting values. The $\mathcal{F}\!\!\mathcal{O}\!\!\mathcal{C}\!\!\mathcal{U}\!\!\mathcal{S}$ framework is built upon the foundations of first-order logic, while the underlying mathematical theorems developed within this research can be leveraged to create efficient algorithms for solving specific consistency-related challenges, such as the repair problem. The $\mathcal{F}\!\!\mathcal{O}\!\!\mathcal{C}\!\!\mathcal{U}\!\!\mathcal{S}$ framework is

This research develops a novel model, called time-dependent Poisson autoregression, to better understand and analyze discrete time series data. A novel hypothesis testing method, based on the score process, is introduced to assess the stationarity of the model. We establish the score process's asymptotic behavior under both time-independent and time-varying conditions, which forms the basis of our inference approach. We prove that, under specific conditions, the model is uniquely identified and consistent estimation is achievable. A specific, more general case is examined, leading to an optimal estimation method for regression parameters. Specifically, it is shown that traditional estimation methods may be suboptimal and inefficient in certain scenarios. Simulations demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed time-dependent model and scoring method. We utilize real-world data, specifically global coal production, to illustrate the method's application.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel representation that equates to 3D object models capable of addressing robust 3D-3D correspondence problems. NDFs consist of directional descriptor vectors attached to the surface of a reference shape, which serves as part of the complete parameter space. This structure facilitates the use of existing, complex-shaped 3D models in place of primitive shapes like spheres. We integrate an $SE(3)$-equivariant field on top of the shape degrees of freedom to complement the base model. This combination is beneficial in applications like medical image segmentation and allows for more accurate matching than descriptor fields based on rotation only. Our work includes a comprehensive evaluation of NDFs on multiple datasets, demonstrating their efficacy in various tasks including image segmentation, pose estimation, and object matching.

The SiD Detector is one of two integrated detector designs being developed for the future linear linear collider, specifically designed to detect particles in the central region and a significant portion of the beam pipe. To complement the ATLAS-CMS experiments, which operate with hadron detectors, the SiD and CALO detectors will provide precise measurements of leptons, photons, and hadrons. This comprehensive system will offer substantial improvements in momentum measurement, featuring a novel silicon tracker with an outer radius of under two meters and an advanced electromagnetic calorimeter featuring fine segmentation for photons, with a radial depth of nearly three meters. This design will enable the detection of neutral hadrons, enabling more effective search strategies for new physics at the ILC. A modified detector design, which reduces the radius to approximately 1.05 meters without compromising performance, has been proposed, incorporating a advanced calorimeter system called the ATLAS Topological Calorimeter (ATC), which offers a unique approach to particle detection by grouping adjacent modules into larger cells. This design features a highly efficient photon detection cell, which maintains good energy resolution while significantly reducing hit multiplicity, enabling effective jet energy resolution and notable time-of-flight particle separation capabilities. This concept has been thoroughly simulated and its design parameters optimized to ensure the detector's capabilities are fully utilized.

Researchers examined the red giant branch stars in the globular cluster Tonantzintla 2, utilizing data from the Cluster APOgee Survey. They discovered that despite having a relatively low mass range of 0.76 to 0.84 times that of the Sun, the cluster exhibits a significant metallicity division. Specifically, the cluster's blue and red populations differ by approximately 0.5 to 1.0 in log[Fe/H]. When examining the average properties, the cluster displays a moderate separation in both metallicity and $\alpha$-process element abundances on the red giant branch, with an average metallicity difference of 0.9 in log[Fe/H], an average $\alpha$-process element abundance difference of 0.15, and an average magnesium abundance difference of 0.07. Furthermore, the research indicates a possible correlation between higher metallicity and $\alpha$-process element abundance. Although the exact origin of this correlation remains unclear, it could be attributed to a division in the cluster's stellar population or represent a feature seen in some other galactic globular clusters.

The growth of library-based software has significantly contributed to the complexity of its system, resulting in a necessitation for enhanced testing, verification, and analysis methods. With substantial libraries having become prevalent in recent years, this challenge has accelerated in pace. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs now encompasses over 150 projects and spans more than 30 domains, ranging from modeling to analysis and multiple testing approaches. To facilitate quicker discovery of specific proofs or features within the AFP, a novel search framework is proposed, which employs semantic rather than syntactic criteria to facilitate more intuitive queries, much like real programmers understand their code. This framework leverages the power of LISP to facilitate the creation of a range of search functions, from straightforward text-based searches to sophisticated, domain-specific algorithms. As an example of its capabilities, a new index for multiset ordering is proposed, which, at a rate of 0.001 seconds, outperforms the existing best index by a margin of 74.4 times, demonstrating the potential for further optimization within the framework.

Recently, researchers have made significant efforts to connect the physics of quantum mechanics and quantum field theory to statistical mechanics, using quantum magnets as a model. These efforts have led to intriguing findings related to the Yang-Lee edge singularity (YLES), where conventional understanding breaks down. In this study, we investigate systematic methods for measuring the Yang-Lee edge singularity in classic, non-quantum, and non-trivial, self-interacting, symmetric (O(N)) universality classes. By analyzing magnetization values at critical points in lattice models, we develop a consistent method for determining the self-interacting, symmetric (O(N)) universality class of the Yang-Lee edge singularity. Our research shows that this method yields reliable results across a range of theories, providing insight into the underlying physics of these systems.

In statistics and machine learning, the "easier than random" and "locally easier than globally" principles are fundamental concepts that underpin many state-of-the-art algorithms, particularly message passing algorithms like approximate message passing (AMP). This paper presents two key results: an improved bound on the second moment of AMP dynamics, which is more precise than previous findings and suitable for applications "easier than random"; and an essential property of AMP, "locally easier than global", which is now formally established. Leveraging this property, along with the enhanced bound, this paper provides the first rigorous proof of the local curvature of the TAP free energy, a discovery made earlier but without a formal validation. Additionally, it is shown that the combination of "locally easier than global" and the increased second-moment bound of AMP leads to the emergence of magnetization cycles in the AMP-TAP iteration, which is in turn simpler than global, and simplifies the analysis of local convergence, yielding additional insights such as the existence and absolute continuity of the Gibbs measure's support.

Modern metasurfaces, at the intersection of advanced technology and science,  
constitute an intricate field that can manipulate electromagnetic waves effectively  
by integrating multiple layers within an ultra-thin depth, nevertheless,  
investigating this complex system poses significant challenges due to its sensitive  
requirements and interconnected variables. To overcome these obstacles, we have  
developed a cutting-edge computational framework that integrates full-wave  
simulations and rational approximation to investigate the comprehensive response  
of metasurfaces across a wide frequency spectrum. This approach enables us to assess  
their theoretical capabilities in filtering, wave shunting, and wave manipulation,  
with particular emphasis on practical considerations such as power, speed, and  
efficiency. To illustrate the effectiveness of this method, we have examined a  
notch filter based on magnetic ensembles, exploring its performance through  
simulations and experimental evidence. Furthermore, we have explored how this  
approach can be utilized to design bespoke metasurfaces tailored to specific  
applications.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization of autonomous vector fields that have been characterized by a comprehensive set of invariant manifolds in a neighborhood of an non-singular equilibrium point. This goal is achieved by establishing the necessary and sufficient conditions for the orbital linearization of such fully integrable vector fields. Furthermore, a simplified version of the condition exists specifically for analysis near an elementary singularity.

Although complete configuration interaction methods are computationally prohibitive for applications to complex atoms and molecules, they serve as reference standards for next-generation quantum computers. In this study, we demonstrate a novel, exponentially efficient approach to CI using an asymmetric normalizing flow, which can learn a parameter set for a variational Coulomb matrix model. This method yields flexible electron correlation wave functions at a polynomial cost, reducing computation requirements for complex systems with many atoms. By training this method on lithium dimers, we obtain accurate results even in cases with extensive electron correlation. This model's capacity to produce accurate configurations may have broad implications for reducing the complexity of calculations on emerging quantum computers.

This study reveals a previously unreported unconnected mass structure, which we call the Massive Arc on the Sky, spanning 1.6 gigaparsecs. We've analyzed nearly 3.4 million galaxies from the KiDS-100 and LSST DR9 surveys, utilizing their positions and redshifts along with mass estimates. By examining these data through various methods and simulations, we've identified this massive structure. It appears to be a linear formation, possibly预示着 filaments that often serve as cradles for large-scale cosmic structures. The Massive Arc on the Sky exhibits a clear mass excess exceeding 6 times the expectation, which stands out even when considering brightness or spatial distribution of galaxies. We've named this remarkable discovery the Massive Arc on the Sky.

While photometric monitoring of stars has a long history in the study of variable stars and supernovae, the full potential of this technique has long been underutilized in the context of atmospheric research. In recent years, the scientific community has increasingly recognized the value of ground-based optical photometry in the assessment of the aerosol component of the atmospheric vertical profile. Ground-based photometric systems have demonstrated the capability to provide continuous, wide-area monitoring of the atmosphere's aerosol component, complementing other measurement techniques such as satellite imaging, radar, and chemical transport modeling. These systems have proven particularly effective in tracking the evolution of aerosol clouds following volcanic eruptions and in monitoring the seasonal and daily patterns of natural aerosol formations. In this review, we discuss recent using photometric data to probe the atmospheric profile, detailing the primary challenges and the photometric systems that have demonstrated the ability to generate reliable photometric data for atmospheric research, including the AERo-POJ system and the data from these systems are used to study the evolution of aerosol clouds following major volcanic eruptions at Kilauea in 2021, Etna in 2021-2023, and Fuego in May-June 2018, as well as seasonal and daily patterns of aerosol formations in the Mediterranean Sea, characterized by distinct photometric variations due to changes in aerosol loads.

Recently, estimating a object's 6D pose using deep learning has made significant advancements, yet the task remains a major challenge in robotics applications, mainly due to the difficulty of collecting large-scale labeled datasets for position-angle prediction. A common workaround involves initially estimating 3D position and orientation separately, although this task is complicated as it requires training neural networks to handle 6D data effectively. In response, we introduce an innovative approach utilizing Deep Correspondence Learning to convert hierarchical feature maps from 3D to 2D, enabling successful 6D pose prediction directly. Furthermore, we integrate this approach with existing methods that project clustered points, resulting in high-performance outcomes on diverse datasets including CWP, NPU-VR, and PoseBay2020. Our models achieve state-of-the-art results on these benchmarks, including record accuracy on the challenging PoseBay2020 dataset with a mean average error (MAP) of 9.34, outperforming existing methods even after the preliminary projection clustering step.

Peridynamics, a novel numerical methodology for analyzing continuous bodies' motion, has gained traction in structural mechanics and damage propagation studies. Recent research has extended peridynamics to dynamic fluid flows and complex flows involving interacting particles and structures, however, there's scant information on the underlying mathematical and physical principles of nonlocal theories of fluid dynamics. This study explores and compares various nonlocal models, including a Bond-based Peridynamic model for analyzing fluid dynamics, and highlights both their shared features and unique characteristics. Although Bond-based Peridynamics offers significant benefits in predicting material behavior, further investigations are needed to better understand its application to fluid-flow problems.

We introduce GGLasso, a Python library designed to address the Universal Graphical Lasso (UGLaSS) problem, which has various applications in analyzing high-dimensional datasets. Specifically, reconstructing a precision matrix from an incomplete positive definite matrix and a set of edge constraints is key to handling missing data in Gaussian variables. Our package builds upon R's GLaSS library and employs a cutting-edge algorithm called ISLA to solve UGLaSS problems efficiently. Additionally, GGLasso includes functions for missing data reconstruction, network visualization, and incorporates examples for a smoother user experience.

Numerous statistical mechanics problems in Biology require understanding the vast, complex free energy landscapes of molecular configurations. By integrating over specific degrees of freedom, lower dimensional effective landscapes can be mapped out, highlighting crucial configurations and their interconnections. For instance, Scylla and Charybda landscapes represent the folding and translation paths of ribosomes reading mRNA, while the landscape of G-quadruplex formation from four guanine-rich strands is particularly rugged due to its multiple possible structures. To navigate these intricate landscapes, stochastic dynamics models, such as Langevin Dynamics (LD), are employed to sample configurations, but this can be hampered by trapping in local minima. To address this, we study the mixing time of LD in terms of landscape features, specifically the depth and size of minima, and the distances between their peaks, as seen in the dynamics' diffusion process. Our theoretical bounding formulas are supported by numerical simulations of particles in double well landscapes and molecular simulations of the trimerization of pyrimidine bases (TC3). In LD with optimal parameters, we observe a significant reduction in the energy exploration time (from O(E^2) to O(E^3/2)) compared to non-optimal scenarios (from O(10^4) to O(10^2) diffusion lengths), while yielding results consistent with rough molecular simulations and traditional simulations in double well landscapes.

Numerical relativity simulations of binary black hole collisions in dark matter environments have largely focused on isolating the effects of dark matter. To comprehensively understand binary black hole collisions, a single point mass model no longer suffices. This affects not just the quantity used to parameterize the binary black hole system, such as the reduced mass, but also the initial conditions, including the choice of baryotropic index for matter around the binary black hole system. Building upon previous work, this study presents an improved version of the simulation code, incorporating a more sophisticated version, and further investigates the effects of dark matter on binary black hole collisions, running additional simulations to compare the results with those using a simpler model. The outcome reveals that a more refined model yields reduced halo density near the binary black hole system and a reduced binary black hole density due to increased accretion, resulting in a significant difference in the final density by a factor of about 10^4. This study's findings highlight the importance of dark matter model and initial conditions in binary black hole collisions, with a more realistic model producing a distinct outcome compared to a simpler model.

Consider an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam composed of $N$ segments connected at various angles, lying in separate planes. This type of structure is commonly employed in modeling multiple interconnected components, such as in an overhead transmission line with transverse shocks affecting specific portions. We investigate the long-term stability of this system when one middle beam is supported by viscous dampers at its endpoints. Using methods of semi-group theory and direct verification, it is shown that closed-form expressions can be derived for the decay rates associated with the system's exponential decay. Specifically, the decay rates can be determined by solving simple algebraic equations, and these rates apply to all modes under certain conditions on the graph's geometry. However, if these conditions are not met, the system exhibits suboptimal energy decay, following a power law, even with infinite gap angles.

Photoacoustic tomography (PAT) systems typically employ acoustic lenses to concentrate energy during energy-deposition, thereby improving the quality of generated ultrasound waves and reducing the required input energy. Nevertheless, conventional PAT setups with wide detection areas don't utilize acoustic lenses due to their tendency to restrict the sampled frequency range of microscopic structures. This research introduces an innovative porous polymeric material with sonic lens properties, allowing for acoustic concave lenses to be used in multi-element PAT arrays with larger detection areas. The sonic lens material exhibits nearly zero sound speed, resulting in concave lenses that effectively convert incident acoustic waves into convex shapes. A simulated 3D PAT system with 120 elements in a circular configuration with a 200 mm diameter was created to test the efficacy of these porous polymeric lenses in improving data acquisition. The simulation revealed a 20 mm diameter improvement in the sampled frequency range of the microstructures when using the porous polymeric lenses compared to not using any type of lens, as measured by the half bandwidth method. The increase in the sampled frequency range was attributed to the conversion of the acoustic waves' shape by the lenses, which resulted in more linear array elements sampling more microstructures with higher frequencies. The proposed porous polymeric material may provide a viable novel material for sonic lenses in PAT systems with larger detection areas.

The growing complexity of modern technology has led to multiple interconnected networks, which can be modeled as dependent, multilayer systems. A new approach to measuring node centrality in these networks has been proposed, accounting for the relationships between layers. Our method uses a weighted adjacency matrix that incorporates both interlayer connections and node importance across different layers. A corresponding eigenvector approach is used to efficiently calculate node centrality scores. We applied this method to analyze the structure of a multilayer network representing the organizational chart of a university, providing insights into key roles within the system.

We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking in noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly.  In response to motion artifacts that commonly occur in raw images, we utilize an end-to-end trainable model called LDD (Joint Demosaicking, Deblurring), which simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs raw images.  LDD takes the motion artifact into account by incorporating an explicit motion model into its demosaicking module through a sampling operation guided by a known motion pattern.  Moreover, LDD employs a newly developed joint loss function that balances the contributions of demosaicking and deblurring losses to the overall loss.  LDD's performance can be further enhanced through deconvolution-based deblurring and demosaicking, as well as curve-of-changes modeling in the temporal domain.  We conduct comprehensive experiments to validate LDD's effectiveness in handling raw images affected by motion.

Recently, we derived the Dirac equation within the Lie derivative framework,
which resulted in an invariant form. In this work, we investigate the structure
of positive energy solutions in $R$-Minkowski spacetime using the derived
equation. Furthermore, we establish the connection between solutions in the Lie
derivative framework and their standard counterparts in $R$-Minkowski spacetime.

This paper introduces the Causal Exploration Toolbox (CAT), a set of methods for analyzing causal connections. As machine learning models grow in complexity, it becomes challenging to grasp their causal dynamics. Although existing approaches offer some solutions, they are often limited to specific situations. Our framework is designed to be adaptable and extensible, with a focus on exploring and visualizing causal connections in Python using domain-specific languages. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness by applying it to a set of standard benchmark examples. Furthermore, we invite contributions from the community to continue developing CAT.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the condition where an air trap forms and maintains stability, preventing water from reaching the sphere's peak. The range of velocities for which this phenomenon occurs has not yet been fully understood. The current research refines the measurable velocity range for this water seal phenomenon to begin below 3 meters per second. The study includes the analysis of high-speed video footage and adjusted velocity measurements to support this finding. The observations were made using spheres of 12.7, 25.4, and 50.8 millimeters in diameter. The study's results suggest a correlation between velocity and the time it takes for an air trap to form, lasting at least 25 milliseconds. The study indicates that increased sphere speed results in longer durations for which the air trap remains intact. The research does not provide a theoretical explanation but rather an empirical observation. The study's findings suggest a relationship between seal pressure within the air trap and dynamic water pressure, exhibiting similar behavior to previously reported results. The research indicates that higher speeds allow seal pressure to match dynamic water pressure. The study's findings provide crucial information for the design of water-based systems such as parachutes, projectiles, and landing mechanisms.

In a Type IIB vacuum expectation state, we investigate the structure of an $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity theory in four dimensions, which results from compactifying maximally supersymmetric Type IIB supergravity by a torus of size two. The 64-component Type IIB gravitino splits into two pairs of Dirac ferminos within four-dimensional supersymmetry. However, a non-trivial symmetry breaking pattern is required to reduce the symmetry to this $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity. This requirement eliminates the possibility of a Lagrangian description for the low-energy effective field theory. Instead, we use a prepotential to define a Lagrangian subsector that is coupled to a non-Lagrangian sector. This supergravity theory contains multiple $U(1)$ gauge symmetries that are associated with the duality group $PSU(1,1)$ in four dimensions. These symmetries lead to the appearance of multiple generalized Witten effects and thus theta-terms within the holomorphic prepotential. The structure of these theta-terms provides insight into the non-Lagrangian sector of the supergravity theory. This analysis is carried out within the context of a maximally supersymmetric Type IIB compactification by tori of size two, which yields a four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity with specific properties.

We present an innovative security architecture, known as SHU (Solely-Used Hardware), which minimizes reliance on trust in this cutting-edge, single-purpose hardware. Traditionally, trust has been circumvented via security hardware, secret storage, or secure processing, yet these methods come with significant overhead in terms of trust. SHU (Solely-Used Hardware) draws from the concept of security derived from complexity, enabling users to depend only on the fundamental, unalterable laws of physics, with no additional trust requirements. This approach, however, does come with a limitation: it necessitates a level of computational security, making it unsuitable for storing high-security information.

In the fields of machine learning and data science, organizations are facing increasing pressure from cyberattacks and insider threats that manipulate training data with significant scale and intensity. To tackle this challenge in policy optimization problems, we developed a resilient policy gradient algorithm capable of combating deceptive data manipulation. By introducing a dual-network architecture consisting of a primary network and a secondary network trained on adjacent training batches, the algorithm distinguishes between legitimate and manipulative data. A innovation called the "trust policy" enables the weight transfer from the primary network to the secondary network, allowing the latter to learn from only authentic data and inform the primary network about malicious data. Theoretical and experimental results show that our algorithm can fulfill resilience criteria and outperform existing methods in terms of robust accuracy.

We introduce a novel type of hypothesis testing game, the $\epsilon$-box game, and prove that under certain conditions (choice and large sample size), a novel form of paradox emerges, effectively demonstrating a rejection of the underlying measure. The concept of the $\epsilon$-box game can be viewed as a modified version of the original box game, and it shares the property of providing a method to decide hypotheses on infinite sequences without, however, being entirely equivalent. Unlike the basic $\epsilon$-box game, a decisive outcome represents the rejection of the underlying measure rather than merely favoring it. Furthermore, the $\epsilon$-box game exhibits the capacity to reject both major and minor hypotheses, including infinitely many, when given sufficient data. The $\epsilon$-box game also exhibits the characteristic of inducing an acyclic preference among three hypotheses under certain conditions, and this decision-making process can be achieved without the aid of choice, contrary to the conventional approach. The introduction of the $\epsilon$-box game serves a unique purpose in addressing concepts that cannot be effectively explored through standard $\delta$-approximation methods.

Cubanite, a cu-Fe sulfide with a nested rock salt structure, exhibits multiple magnetic phases due to the presence of two distinct magnetic ions, cu and Fe. Experimental evidence, such as from specific heat, ac susceptibility, and x-ray absorption spectroscopy, suggests that this material may be a candidate for studying orbital-selective ferromagnetism. A theoretical analysis, utilizing full-band and DFT+U models, reveals that orbital-selective ferromagnetism emerges under certain conditions. Furthermore, this phenomenon intensifies as the Hubbard U for Fe increases, with ferromagnetic order becoming more pronounced in the occupied 3d states, potentially making cubanite an ideal material for verifying this elusive magnetic behavior.

In this research, we observed significant, periodic changes in the coupling strength between a pair of coupled quantum dots and a microwave photon. These variations, known as Rabi oscillations, are not caused by external factors but rather result from external control of the electron spin state through a laser. Notably, the Rabi fluctuations allow for the Rabi frequency to vary over a substantial range - up to three times - without the influence of a external magnetic field.

In a two-dimensional non-symmorphic wallpaper network lattice, Dirac points naturally arise due to its high symmetry, providing an opportunity to manipulate them through tuning. A generalized tight-binding model reveals that, under specific conditions, these points emerge as the result of two linear crossing bands with opposing group velocities. Notably, in a square lattice, points appear when one band surpasses the other, while in other wallpaper lattices, they coincide when the bands are equal. The model also demonstrates that these points can persist regardless of mass term perturbations, owing to its chiral and valley symmetry. By adjusting lattice parameters, we can control the positions of these points, offering a unique pathway for achieving topological phase transitions with a simple design. A quasi-three-dimensional superlattice is then proposed, where the model demonstrates that valley-dependent Floquet-Bessel components give the point non-trivial character, allowing for the generation of both type-1 and type-2 anomalous Dirac cones.

Quantum states that are superpositions of different photon numbers exhibiting relative phase shifts between components are called phase-covariant and are highly beneficial in achieving precise measurements and communicating securely. Although typically created using electronic devices, our approach employs quantum-optical methods to generate these states by combining strong laser light with a single photon, both coupled with non-linear processes. Our models produce states with significant overlap (0.81-0.95) and a non-gaussian character (0.15-0.35), and when detected through standard methods, they exhibit a clear loss of symmetry in their distribution, indicating a level of security suitable for communicating privately. Furthermore, our generated states can demonstrate quantum advantages in communication tasks, surpassing what could be accomplished with just discrete phases or number states.

In General Relativity, using the Newman-Penrose formalism allows us to break down the Weyl tensor into five complex components, which can be understood by analyzing the bivectors of the electromagnetic field and itself. This relationship between these components and the Newman-Penrose components reveals the connection between the electromagnetic field and Weyl curvature in a detailed way. Specifically, we observe how the Newman-Penrose components of the Weyl tensor relate to the principal null directions of an algebraically special electromagnetic field, providing a clear picture of this connection. Furthermore, in the context of vacuum spacetimes, the same analysis reveals how the Weyl tensor components using the Newman-Penrose formalism can be expressed in a detailed form. This can be achieved by expanding a product of bivectors of self-dual electromagnetic field and its conjugate in a basis of irreducible tensors, which includes the Newman-Unterstein operator, and understanding its action on a generic self-dual quadratic form of a spinor. This understanding is also supported by a parallel analysis in Minkowski space using the Newman-Penrose formalism and a similar expansion of bivectors of a self-dual Maxwell field and its conjugate, which can be achieved by applying a similar operator in a flat spacetime context. A polymer is a complex entity composed of numerous repeating molecular units, or monomers, strung together. Due to its vast composition, accurately determining a polymer's chemical structure from a given sample can be a challenging task. While mass spectrometry has been commonly employed for this purpose, its application to larger molecules like polymers poses significant difficulties. To overcome these difficulties, our proposed method utilizes an approach based on nonnegative integer linear regression to decode the composition of a polymer from mass spectrometry data. By predicting the counts of possible monomers as a function of additive additives, this method successfully recovers the full chemical structure of the polymer. Our method has been successfully tested on a variety of polymer samples, demonstrating its capability to derive chemical structures that align with existing literature and, in some cases, provide more detailed information than previously known.

This paper provides an in-depth explanation of a direct transcription method for creating optimized schedules in complex systems subject to significant uncertainties. We demonstrate how this method can be employed to create optimal ventilation schedules for a hospital, taking into account various possible COVID-19 transmission patterns and the need to balance treatment quality and safety. By formulating a direct transcription problem as a high-dimensional nonlinear optimization issue, we develop a solution that remains effective under a range of COVID-19 scenarios and minimizes unnecessary variations in airflow. Additionally, this paper explores the challenges of solving such problems using advanced optimization techniques, including gradient-based methods, neural network approximations, and a step-by-step solution to a simplified ventilation case.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus through computed tomography (CT) imaging and combining visual inspection with this method is a reliable technique for esophageal tumor segmentation.  As the complexity of CT images rises, directly applying this combined approach can lead to suboptimal results due to the limited contrast between the esophagus and surrounding tissues.  To effectively outline the inner lumen of an esophagus with complex structures, our focus DDAUnet model leverages pre-processing steps to simplify CT image analysis and utilizes dilated dense attention blocks to accurately capture both local and remote features.  Our experiments utilizing three public datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of precision, recall, and overall F1-score.

This study is an investigation into well log analysis and uncertainty quantification using an ensemble approach, with particular relevance to geosteering. A key contribution of this research is the development of a new method for calculating cross-well covariance through the use of deep learning techniques. To obtain predictions with reliable statistics and a efficient way to model complex, non-Gaussian distributions of target properties, we trained stochastic deep learning models on synthetic data generated using Monte Carlo methods. A novel approach to these calculations is the use of ensemble methods, which allow us to compute the cross-well covariance directly, avoiding the need for time-consuming simulations. To show the practical application of this method, we used a synthetic dataset to demonstrate how this approach can be used to estimate target properties and their uncertainties, with a focus on their use in well planning and geosteering. A key contribution of this research is the development of a new method for calculating cross-well covariance through the use of deep learning techniques, which allows us to predict properties and their uncertainties more accurately and efficiently than traditional methods. To further explore the potential of this approach, we used a real-world dataset to demonstrate how this method can be used to estimate target properties and their uncertainties, with a focus on their use in well planning and geosteering. To accurately model the uncertainty of predictions and avoid the problem of underestimating the variance of predictions, we used a new method based on the average and variance of ensemble predictions, which has a clear theoretical basis and is more

Named entity recognition (NER) is a vital task in natural language processing and many other applications rely on it. NER can also uncover the hierarchical structure of sentences, which can be used for text understanding. This paper proposes a new approach to evaluate the ability of NER models to parse the comprehensive structure of sentences, which includes nested entities. We introduce a new metric called Nested NER Comprehensiveness Score (NCTS) to quantify this parsing capability, and encourage researchers to report it in future studies. Our experiments on three datasets, including two base ones and a domain-adaptive task, show that current NER models, particularly those based on linear sequence tagging, struggle to accurately parse nested entities, indicating a need for further research to enhance their ability to handle complex, nested structures.

We utilize the tropicalization of a generic plane quartic to:
  - increase the readability of existing proofs demonstrating the existence of a
    non-empty set of bitangents to a plane quartic over fields of characteristic
    zero, with a large uniformizing parameter and a valuation;
  - provide an $\mathbb{A}^1$-count for the ensemble of bitangents to a plane quartic using
    operations including Sch\"afer's valuation, Milnor-Kato sign, and Milnor K-theory depth.
    Furthermore, we establish conditions on the sign and depth of this count that are
    applicable to the number of bitangents over a field of a sufficiently high positive
    characteristic, as well as the real signed count.

Research into the location detection of target nodes through signal measurement and processing, based on the use of short-range radio technologies like Low Energy IEEE 802.15.4 and IEEE 802.11, is heavily dependent on path loss modeling.  A newly proposed hybrid path loss model is introduced, which takes into account not only the exponential decrease in received signal strength but also the influence of cross-technology interference, a common occurrence in sensor networks.  This model is supported by the development of a maximum likelihood estimator for location estimation that efficiently determines target nodes' positions using measurement data collected from reference nodes with known locations.  The effectiveness and accuracy of the location estimation method are verified through theoretical analysis and practical testing in controlled environments.  Findings show that, in the absence of interference, the model's results are as accurate as those using IEEE 802.15.4 networks, while in highly contaminated environments, it outperforms existing linear and non-linear processing techniques.  The location estimation algorithm is also optimized for low computational complexity, making it suitable for real-time implementation.  A dataset consisting of 270 location measurements collected under high levels of IEEE 802.11 interference is utilized to evaluate the algorithm's performance, with outcomes indicating significant accuracy improvements, including up to a 22% increase in 2D RMS error compared to the state of the art.

This paper offers an in-depth examination of the code-switching phenomenon,
which occurs when individuals express a single thought in multiple languages
within sentences that are grammatically correct in each respective language.
Researchers across the globe are undertaking investigations to develop natural
language processing techniques for natural languages, including code-switched
variations. Although there exists existing literature covering code-switching
within specific language pairs, such as Hindi-English and English-Spanish, there
are still numerous aspects requiring in-depth study to fully comprehend the
complexities associated with code-switching. Key components, namely cognitive
and linguistic aspects, as well as their implications for natural language
processing models and current research methodologies, will be explored within
this paper. Additionally, it provides insights into code-switching behavior
within multilingual societies.

Assessing the quality of generated descriptions for images is a significant challenge in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). While human assessment would be most accurate, it's often costly and impractical for large datasets. As a result, many methods employ statistically based metrics to measure similarity between generated and reference descriptions, albeit with limited effectiveness. Given the widespread use of social media platforms for gathering diverse and extensive descriptions, can these collections still serve as reliable standards for evaluating the capabilities of NLP models? This paper scrutinizes the characteristics of such data while also examining their potential to facilitate meaningful comparisons between models.

Tantalum oxides display a range of interesting properties and are found in various forms in nature.  The complex electronic and molecular characteristics of these compounds have drawn significant attention, especially when they appear as nanoparticles or in nanoshell forms.  Despite existing X-ray data on two Ta$_2$O$_5$ phases, the exact atomic lattice arrangements of these phases have not been fully confirmed.  To address this, researchers utilized experimental X-ray data and performed simulations to determine the lattice structures of two tantalum oxide phases, optimizing their energy and comparing them to observed diffraction patterns.  While certain properties of one phase can be explained with a specific lattice arrangement, further analysis is needed to fully confirm its exact atomic lattice arrangement due to the close similarities between two competing models.

Previous research on the spread of misinformation primarily focused on personal, emotional, and cognitively demanding factors. A major socio-technological event, often referred to as "The Big Geographic Shift," happened around 2017 on Reddit when users posted misinformation that matched their location with the origin of the news, reversing the trend where users from different states shared such information. This significant change prompted us to investigate its geographic implications and explore how geographic familiarity affects the propagation of misinformation among Reddit users. Our analysis covered more than six million news articles from 2015 to 2020 and examined their engagement patterns from the perspective of geographic familiarity. Our main findings indicated that geographic familiarity plays a crucial role in limiting the spread of misinformation on Reddit. It also suggested that users were willing to engage with misinformation that originated in unfamiliar places and shared it across those boundaries. Furthermore, our research highlighted how geographic dynamics were influenced by major geographic platforms like Reddit and that these platforms contributed to shaping this influence. Based on these findings, we proposed that external factors, including geographic familiarity and the role of major geographic platforms should be taken into account when studying the spread of misinformation online.

The prevalence of messaging apps like WhatsApp and WeChat among criminals has facilitated deceptive phishing links and suspicious URLs to be disseminated swiftly, making it challenging to identify their presence, especially at high speeds. Traditional methods of detecting such content, mainly based on signature matching, are rendered ineffective due to the rapid copying and modification of data. In response, we introduce a novel, real-time detection approach called Real-time Suspicious Flow Analysis (RSFA) that analyzes the temporal changes in file sizes as suspicious files undergo protocol transformations. By utilizing unsupervised learning techniques, we are able to identify patterns of suspicious incidents in real-time, without the need to pre-determine or list specific types of suspicious content. The efficacy of RSFA has been proven, with our results showing superior performance compared to other methods in detecting various malicious attacks, including phishing HTML documents, cryptolocker binaries, and fake app packages.

The emergence of deep learning-driven robot teaching methods, where human instructors guide robots through tasks by demonstrating actions, has led to a common setup involving a recording station and a execution station. Although this arrangement works for simple tasks using whole-body recordings, it presents efficiency drawbacks, comfort issues for instructors, and limitations on the types of tasks that can be taught due to the need for full-body recordings. These issues motivate the development of more effective human-in-the-loop learning techniques for robots. This paper, however, focuses on the data collected during the recording phase and explores the potential for the instructor to split the task into two parts: having the student robot perform a limited movement, while a human operator guides the robot through a series of targeted movements. This approach paves the way for further research into filtering and processing data in real-time to enhance the ways humans can guide robots through complex tasks.

Tree structures are found in various areas of computer science, including data organization and network routing. Existing research on random trees is limited to trees that adhere to a single organizational principle. A new algorithm has been developed to generate random trees that incorporate multiple-org principles. This algorithm uses a systematic approach to create trees by applying a single-org method to a subset of nodes and then integrating an alternative method to assign inter-node connections. The accuracy and effectiveness of the algorithm have been validated through numerical experiments that show it produces trees whose properties align with theoretical expectations and those generated by alternative methods. Furthermore, the algorithm has been utilized to generate a large dataset of trees for statistical analysis and to derive an efficient estimator for estimating tree height. This estimator outperforms a widely used method based on coalescent theory.

Using the equivalence between two-dimensional conformal field theory and Euler-Arnold equations,
we establish a connection to rigid systems of differential equations.
By leveraging the resulting properties of power series solutions,
we derive second-order differential constraints on conformal field theory components.
These derived constraints allow us to expose the hidden rigidity within the cohomological constraints of conformal field theory.

Next-generation conversational agents are being developed to adapt rapidly to the dynamics of online social interaction, requiring efficient learning models. To ensure the reliability and validity of these models, the creation of automated testing systems is becoming increasingly vital. However, establishing such a system requires a comprehensive set of human-written specifications that can guide the automatic progression of a conversation with a defined outcome. These written scripts serve multiple purposes, including the development of manual prototypes, the generation of human feedback for machine learning model optimization, and most importantly, the development of an accurate reference point for evaluating the automated performance of the learning model. Despite these benefits, the requirement of creating these written scripts becomes a substantial hurdle when tackling more complex conversation topics. To address this challenge, the establishment of a new automated testing system for a learning conversational model is proposed, including the use of the超评价 (ChaoPing) system that facilitates the efficient generation of high-quality human feedback and the accurate assessment of the model's outputs.

Although often referred to as Planet Nine, the hypothetical object beyond Neptune should also be called Planet X, given that it's not the first such celestial body discovered in this region. Various characteristics of the known trans-Neptunian objects and Scattered-Disk-Objects suggest the existence of one or multiple distant massive objects with masses equivalent to Earth's, possibly 3 to 4 such objects could track with the known planets through subtle changes in their orbits induced by gravitational forces. Using a post-Newtonian framework to analyze data from NASA JPL's Horizons system, this study attempted to constrain the mass of these potential objects within a specific distance range (currently known planets to 200 AU) by evaluating the residual signals remaining after removing the effects of the known planets' gravitational interactions. The study found notable constraints on 1 Earth-mass object, confirming previous findings and improving them by a factor of 3 in certain directions. Specifically, the study limited 1 Earth-mass objects to a maximum of approximately 2 to 3 within 200 AU, however it found even more stringent constraints on objects with masses exceeding Earth's, often reaching limits of approximately 0.5 to 1 within 200 a typical distance range for Planet X, often referred to as 2 to 4 units of mass. The study also discovered notable similarity between its results and those obtained via analyzing the orbits of the known planets, with often comparable limits of approximately 0.

To improve translation accuracy, especially for uncommon words, our approach involves pre-training a lexicon memory for the target language. This additional memory allows our model to access frequent target words before generating them, effectively supplementing its prior knowledge. We call this approach Monolingual Lexicon Memory (MLAM), which focuses on translating less common source words. By limiting the use of this lexicon memory, we prevent the model from simply accessing target words that it already knows well. Our method employs a lightweight encoder to access the lexicon memory and uses only a few extra parameters for the additional memory. Experimental results on English-Chinese and German-French translations show improvements in translation quality using BLEU and TER metrics. By sharing our code and models, we invite further exploration and improvement to this approach.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background's temperature and polarization spectra, as well as in the probability distribution of large-scale structures, could indicate the presence of pre-big-bang information. Within the framework of the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model, the author calculates the expected signatures and finds a correlation between the primordial gravitational waves background and the current universe's conformal age. Furthermore, the author determines the expected probability distribution of scalar modes and finds a limitation to the conformal flatness approximation, likely due to a universe that is transitioning from one epoch to the next, causing a scaling of the amplitude of the power spectrum. Due to the similar effects of this transition on sub-horizon and super-horizon scales, the author also predicts a unique signature of pre-big-bang gravitational waves as a background of gravitational anomalies.

This paper builds upon prior work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which introduced and analyzed the Yamabe evolution equation from a dynamic perspective. The primary objective is to prove the convergence of this flow under specific initial conditions. Furthermore, the investigation led to discovering new properties of the Yamabe heat equation.

To efficiently adapt to new situations, humans utilize prototypical examples of existing categories. For instance, when encountering new food, they may order based on a partially completed menu filled with typical dishes. We develop an approach that utilizes one or no labeled examples per category to learn a type that represents the essence of each category. This method, based on neural networks, generates descriptive features from a single image example and learns from a separate set of unlabeled support images. These support images are obtained from additional data without labeling. The method is tested on the mini ImageNet dataset with varying levels of support, and results show that our method outperforms other methods in terms of accuracy.

To tackle the challenge of sparse data in multiple domains for cross-domain recommendation, a cooperative approach is suggested where users from different but related domains work together to enhance their preference knowledge for product rating. This cooperative process involves users from different domains making ratings in their own and related products, with a novel, multi-aspect preference model called Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (ECAP) that aims to capture implicit connections between domains through a more efficient information-sharing mechanism. This model employs a graph attention network to model the relationship between related domains and a dual-pathway design that allows for direct exchange of domain-specific sparse data and indirect sharing of latent features across domains. ECAP also achieves better knowledge transfer of multi-sparsed domain information by effectively combining these implicit domain connections and cooperative ratings. Comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of ECAP in surpassing existing cooperative recommendation methods.

To enhance optimization problem solvers, particularly those involving complex mathematical shapes like cones, we introduce Hypatia, a novel framework written in Julia. This system integrates 20+ state-of-the-art solvers and enables the creation of innovative applications through object-oriented programming. We showcase Hypatia's capabilities by introducing and solving a novel problem related to fluid dynamics, specifically a Poiseuille flow problem, under specific conditions.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, this research develops a method that incorporates private EVs into the planning of grid operations. An agent-based method is created to simultaneously optimize grid restoration and charging of multiple EVs, taking into consideration their individual preferences and needs. This approach is formulated as a collection of interconnected problems that leverage decentralized solution techniques and careful design of grid-restoration strategies. Numerical tests reveal that allowing for flexible use of private EVs can enhance grid resilience by a significant margin. Furthermore, it is found that utilizing private EVs in an uncoordinated manner may lead to overloading of grid components, emphasizing the need for a coordinated approach to grid restoration and EV charging.

Recently, Intel introduced Optane DC Persistent Memory, building on 3D XPoint Technology, which significantly improves memory capacity at a lower cost per gigabyte compared to traditional DRAM. Due to its non-volatile nature, Optane DC PM can retain stored data even after power loss, allowing for faster system recovery and reduced data synchronization during data writes. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of Optane DC PM performance, including latency and throughput measurements for various access methods (load, store, flush) under different paging granularities. The study also explores the potential for developing efficient flash-based main memory systems based on Optane DC PM.

In a bipedal robot that walks on a flat surface, we've developed a system of intrinsic motivation that translates into a meeting schedule between multiple agents within a given area. This system utilizes an episode-based approach, where each meeting represents one episode. For anyone interested in seeing the full details of the project, a corresponding link provides a link to a video showcasing the meeting capabilities of algorithms from different versions of the system. We start by representing each potential meeting as a sequence of actions that form a path, and then apply a recurrent neural network to predict the reward for that path. Ultimately, the network with the highest predicted reward determines the most likely agent to meet at a particular location, and the chosen agent executes the corresponding sequence of actions to reach that location. To optimize efficiency, we utilize transfer learning to speed up the process of discovering high rewards in subsequent episodes, building upon the parameters of the previously successful network.

This paper explores the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.50$, and $0.75$) through theoretical analysis. The study involves examining the full-projection augmented wave method within the density functional theory framework, employing the Rostok magnetic configuration for both GdSn3 and CmSn3. The research reveals that all compounds adopt the Ni$_3$In crystal structure and follow the Gd/Cm atomic arrangement in GdSn3 and CmSn3. The studies of GdSn3 and CmSn3 compounds indicate that they are metallic with predominant p-d hybridization and satisfy the von Mises criteria under applied pressure. The application of 10 GPa of pressure in GdSn3 and 15 GPa of pressure in CmSn3 minimize their unit cell volumes. The magnetic analysis of GdSn3 and CmSn3 compounds with 10 GPa of pressure indicate that they enter the antiferromagnetic state and become half-metallic.
