For the first time, forecasts for other types of baryons and a broader range of mesons are being made using Standard Quantum Chromodynamics (SQCD) principles and existing experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider. This analysis covers an extensive range of central produced particles produced in pairs of jets during collisions at a $\sqrt{s}=1.3$ TeV energy level. The study focuses on identifying all possible mesons consisting of light first-generation quarks (up, down, and strange) and briefly discusses the potential for charmed and bottom-containing particles. The forecasted particle production includes notable examples such as the $\Delta^{++}$, $\Omega^{-}$, and various resonant and non-resonant mesons. The production rates for these particles are being predicted and some degree of experimental verification would provide valuable insight into the underlying SQCD understanding.

We provide a novel, simplified method to identify the fundamental Coxexeder length patterns for both B_n and I_n type Coxeter groups, which can also be applied to find the basic building blocks of group elements.

Utilizing recent estimates for the lensing effect imposed by foreground matter on distant supernovae beyond our galaxy, along with a dataset of Type Ia supernovae in our galaxy that have been associated with foreground matter, providing credibility maps for potential discovery of dark energy, these findings may bolster efforts to identify these phenomena, considering background supernovae are typically 10 to 100 times more faint.

These are lecture notes for a 2022 St. Flour Summer School on Stochastic Partial Differential Equations. 

The material covers fundamental concepts in the theory of stochastic partial differential equations and discusses key examples and recent breakthroughs in the field. 

Given that this is an introductory survey, it focuses heavily on models where significant recent advancements have been made, particularly within the field of regularisation by noise. 

The focus of this research is on parabolic equations driven by space-time white noise. It also briefly touches on hyperbolic equations and random PDEs from geometric topology. 

These topics share underlying connections to stochastic analytic semigroups and Sobolev spaces with negative norms.

A new structure called the T node has been discovered in silicon-on-insulator materials, which can affect how light interacts with it. The T node forms when a defect line develops at the interface between silicon and buried oxide, branching into two nodes perpendicular to the defect and meeting the silicon surface. The position of the T node can be determined using a non-destructive method called photoluminescence, which detects a specific signal originating from the T node. The location of the T node is important to know before manufacturing devices because it can affect their performance. A theoretical model based on stress has been developed to predict where the T node will form, utilizing a method called phase field simulation. Furthermore, an experimental procedure using thermal treatments to induce T nodes without damaging the materials has been demonstrated.

MRI technology utilizes radio waves to generate detailed images of the human body,
making it an effective non-invasive diagnostic tool.  Due to their ability to give
valuable information non-invasively, MRI images are widely employed in medical
decision-making.  However, their volume and complexity can pose a challenge for
human interpretation, requiring advanced imaging processing techniques to extract
essential information.  These techniques, including morphological processing,
edge detection, image segmentation, and texture analysis, enable the extraction of
critical details from medical images.  Their successful application aids healthcare
professionals in making informed diagnostic and treatment decisions.  This project
utilizes a combination of imaging processing techniques to assist medical
specialists in diagnosing brain tumors from MRI images, specifically utilizing an
MRI scan.  The project's source code and accompanying methodology are made available
to other professionals in the medical field.

The algebraic framework introduced in this paper is designed to accommodate multiple variables within a noncommutative, unital setting, and specifically demonstrates that any set of commuting variables can be managed. We have discovered that this framework generalizes previous algebraic methods related to degenerating the Bernoulli and Stirling numbers. As a result, we introduce the concept of multi-degenerate Bernoulli numbers, establish their fundamental properties, provide an explicit formula, and derive recurrence relationships.

The variation in stellar activity across wavelengths complicates the detection of exoplanets using radial velocity methods. Employing spectral regions with few active regions is beneficial for minimizing this noise. This study explores how utilizing different wavelength ranges influences the ability to detect weak planetary signals, assuming we can effectively remove the broad line shifts caused by rotation and the overall spectral energy distribution through deconvolution. It investigates whether the choice of line lists used in this process affects a deconvolved rotation broadened profile and explores options for selecting line lists that can optimize detection sensitivity. Despite attempting to remove the effects of activity and other factors, results show that the resulting deconvolved profiles of different line lists do not fully overlap. However, switching from one list to another after deconvolution produces a similar outcome. Consequently, it implies that at a given signal-to-noise ratio, stellar activity's impact on exoplanet detection may be largely independent of the specific line lists used, as long as they contain a sufficient number of lines. Furthermore, it suggests that, provided they contain a certain number of lines, even arbitrary line lists may yield comparable outcomes. These findings were verified with observations of the Sun and a cool star, for which we also examine the effect of binary systems on the results.

This research proposes a new method for designing a quality link assessment algorithm and a strategy for organizing clusters in a hierarchical manner, all part of an online, request-driven data collection system for a wireless sensor network. The proposed strategy includes: 1) a link quality algorithm using only local information from each sensor node, 2) a set of methods to determine the quality of connections between nodes, also based on available data, 3) a cluster organization system that minimizes the time and energy used for data transmission, 4) analysis of how to choose the starting points for this process, and 5) theoretical insights into the performance of this system. Furthermore, a simulation model was created to test and validate the effectiveness of this approach.

For our task of extracting crucial information from rich multimedia content,
contextualizing deep-detected objects is essential. Building on this need, we
have designed a straightforward yet effective model that integrates scene
information and neighboring object details to the objects identified by
state-of-the-art object detection systems. This particular subsystem is tailored
to operate with any object detector based on region-based convolutional neural
networks, including the famous Fast R-CNE object detector. The additional
information about detected objects is obtained by training separate, compact
classifiers for feature extraction. These classifiers are trained independently
using the same dataset, carefully selecting informative features that aid in
decoding context. In preparation for context localization, we also devised a
relevant labeling method and a specialized training technique called
hierarchical multi-task learning. This technique allows us to train the
detection model and the context localization model jointly, enabling the
former to utilize background information, nearby object details, and target
attributes. In the experiments conducted, this technique resulted in notable
enhancements in object detection accuracy and scene object classification
performance.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are governed by a general Kirchhoff function and a limiting Trudinger-Moser growth, particularly when the system exhibits exponential growth near infinity and polynomial growth near the origin. Furthermore, the research focuses on solutions distinct from trivial zero solutions. By employing a variational approach and critical point theory, the required conditions are met, resulting in either two or three different solution configurations.

We develop detailed, user-friendly upper bounds for the probability of rare events in sums of binary random variables that satisfy specific independence constraints. Our development builds upon work by Angers and Angers, providing a user-friendly version of complex technical proofs. We demonstrate the utility of these new bounds in establishing concentration inequalities and useful corollaries related to quadiagonal matrices and the entropy method.

Given a Noetherian ring $A$ with characteristic $p > 0$, we've constructed equivalent categories of modules over the crystal ring associated to a supersingular $p$-adic string, maintaining preservation of important properties like isomorphism and attitude. This crystal module category features finite presentation and satisfies compact generation. It's relatively semistable over the crystal ring, with each relative crystal module displaying a simple relative Dieudonne theory. Notably, this holds true when the crystal ring is principal ideal domain, enabling an attitude exact sequence for finite presentable crystal modules.

This study explores the possibility of generating a cos$\phi_R$ asymmetry in two-particle production during SIDIS experiments with longitudinally polarized protons, using the helicity dependence of the Collins effect to study this phenomenon. By examining the  SIDIS data from the HERA experiment, specifically from 1994-2001, we found a small but significant signal for the cos$\phi_R$ asymmetry. Contrary to expectations, the observed significance cannot be fully explained by potential biases arising from the alignment of particle pairs. Building on this, we investigated the theoretical cause of this alignment bias by simulating SIDIS data based on various models of spin-dependent fragmentation function and polarization of hadron produced color dipoles. Our research indicates a key discrepancy between existing phenomenological models and a crucial constraint that has not been fully addressed. Additionally, we found that including the Collins effect in our simulations can fully account for the observed cos$\phi_R$ asymmetry in SIDIS data.

Eugene Fock made a significant contribution to general relativity by adapting the metric of de Sitter space into a conformally related form of the Minkowski metric.  Fock achieved this by applying four specific harmonic coordinate transformations to the static de Sitter metric.  When applying similar transformations to the Fock's de Sitter metric, the coordinate system becomes equivalent to the global de Sitter coordinate system, which can be represented as a four-dimensional sphere moving through time.  The conformal factor of the de Sitter metric in this coordinate system is exactly equal to one-fourth of the cosmological constant, provided it is greater than zero.  This research extends understanding of de Sitter space by connecting different coordinate systems and highlighting the properties of its conformal factor.

Given a symplectic manifold, a Lie subgroup of its diffeomorphism group preserves the symplectic form if it undergoes a symplectic transformation. This condition can be met by ensuring the subgroup lies within the stabilizer of the symplectic form and satisfies the isotropy version of Lie's first fundamental theorem. We explore this by examining specific examples, including rotations in $\mathbb R^{2n}$, although their diffeomorphism group does not conform to the expected criterion despite being a large Lie subgroup. Furthermore, we investigate subgroups that convert pairs of compatible complex structures into each other, with some having the same symmetry as the orthogonal group. This allows us to establish the identical modular spaces for a given complex structure, with potential implications for SYZ hyperkähler geometry.

This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an e-rank index, derived from the hierarchical structure of Wikipedia. By applying a hierarchical grouping method to Wikipedia's layered graph, we effectively reduce its complexity while preserving crucial information. This efficient representation enables rapid retrieval of recommended entities. Experimental evaluations on the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph demonstrate that our approach outperforms both non-hierarchical and non-Wikipedia-based baseline models. Furthermore, a comparative analysis with Wikipedia's own recommendation system further validates our model's effectiveness.

Furthermore, this paper's findings are visually depicted through visualizations of the recommended entities' hierarchical structure of Wikipedia.

The increasing number of patients on the waiting list for transplants highlights the need to utilize available transplants more effectively. Specifically, abandoned kidneys that are removed from donation candidates due to medical complications or other reasons are being overlooked, with potential for recovery and use. These kidneys are rarely considered, with only a few programs having success stories. Given their limited supply, it's crucial to employ them strategically to maximize the overall supply of transplants. We develop a mathematical model to determine the optimal course of action for these kidneys, considering both immediate and long-term benefits. Analytical solutions are derived for various scenarios, and numerical applications explore the impact of kidney condition and treatment costs on decision-making. Our research also identifies the potential value of investing in saving these kidneys.

The current overfitting challenge in Deep Learning has led to the emergence of Implicit Tie architectures, which offer a promising solution by sharing parameters across layers in a hierarchical manner. In this review, we provide the first comprehensive overview of this innovative approach in Deep Learning. Starting with Implicit Tie Neural Networks, this concept has been extended to Complex Valued Implicit Tie Networks and Implicit Tie Networks, each addressing specific limitations and challenges. This review also explores the existing Implicit Tie-related approaches in Deep Learning and highlights the need for further research to overcome current challenges and unlock the full potential of these architectures.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We evaluate whether the learned word representations genuinely capture linguistic categories identified by Loughran and McDonald in their seminal work on identifying negative and positive concepts within corporate disclosures. Our thorough analysis, encompassing both textual semantics and statistical text generation aspects, reveals significant shortcomings of the model. Although it excels at generating context for subsequent words, our research reveals that embedded words do not accurately reflect distinct semantic categories. Moreover, our empirical analysis shows that certain grammatical categories are easily distinguishable via vector projections, while others, such as positive and negative concepts, are not. Notably, our findings indicate that despite word2vec's proficiency in predicting context, embedded words are often indistinguishable from randomly selected vocabulary. These results suggest that the word2vec model, particularly the Skip-gram variant, is deficient in capturing distinct semantic categories, likely due to its focus on co-occurrence information rather than context. Given these limitations, we advise caution against relying on embedded texts generated by word2vec models. To facilitate future advancements, we have made our evaluation datasets publicly available to encourage open research.

This paper presents the solutions for multiple antenna and multiple carrier systems that mirror our previous research on integrated data and energy transfer using shaped waveforms. We derive closed-form expressions for optimal performance in a wide range of scenarios with multiple antennas and carrier frequencies, and investigate the underlying relationships and patterns in these expanded systems. Additionally, this paper creates connections to shaped-OFDM and provides practical insights for implementing this technology in real-world applications. A numerical example is provided to validate the findings and highlight the extra gain provided by multiple antennas and multiple carriers.

A new computational method is introduced to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By using a level-set function to track the boundary between solid and liquid, and implementing the embedded boundary method within a grid-based framework, this approach effectively handles extreme deformation, branching, and merging of the interface. The method was tested with various interface shapes and the results showed efficient and accurate calculations, with a significant reduction in computational time through the use of a higher resolution grid for the solid phase.

Current versions of the Lambek Calculus are effective tools for analyzing language,
yet they are limited to handling only contextual information. To improve the
calculus, one can incorporate basic features of natural language, such as the
concept of superposition, which allows for multiple states to be represented in
a single entity, and the unary modality, often referred to as the "spin" connective,
which encodes these states. By integrating these features, we can develop an
extended resource-sensitive logical system that expands beyond the standard
Lambek Calculus, and potentially, a corresponding extended type-ambiguous
grammar. This innovative approach may provide a more nuanced framework for
analyzing linguistic phenomena, and offers the possibility of uncovering new
insights into the relationship between syntax and semantics, particularly in
areas where traditional models struggle to offer clear explanations, such as the
interplay between contextual and extrinsic semantic components.

Deep learning-based predictors have effectively surpassed human expertise in many games by extensively training on vast datasets. However, due to lack of prior knowledge about game mechanics, the strategies used to beat human players often lack interpretability. To address this issue, researchers have developed methods to derive human-comprehensible strategies, though these approaches usually focus on simple games played by two opponents. In multiplayer games, the concept of equilibrium, which describes a strategy that no participant wishes to alter, plays a crucial role. This concept is challenging to apply to the strategies of the games in question. Building on existing research, this work presents a method for determining the strategies of two opponents that are both easily interpretable and form an unstable equilibrium. The proposed approach involves a novel, agnostic way to transform the games that the strategies operate on, along with an equilibrium-sensitive loss function to guide the training of the methods. Experimental evaluations on several well-known games demonstrate the proposed method's efficacy in generating strategies that exceed the performance level of the original strategies used to beat human opponents and are capable of forming the equilibrium with the original games. Furthermore, this method can also be applied to derive the strategies of more than two players, making it a versatile approach for deriving the strategies of the games in question.

A study was conducted using a nonMarkovian SIR model to analyze how a preventive rewiring rule can affect the spread of epidemics on complex networks. In this model, individuals who are infected are removed from the network, while those who recover form new connections. Conversely, susceptible vertices that form a link with an infectious one without becoming infected themselves create the epistatic edges responsible for shaping the network's dynamics. The researchers utilized the generating function formalism to derive a set of differential equations that describe the evolution of the network and an appropriate SIR model to analyze this process. Their findings revealed that introducing the rewiring rule can significantly alter the network's properties, potentially containing the spread of an epidemic even when susceptibility for forming new connections is higher than for establishing interactive contacts. The study also found that the rules governing the formation of interactive contacts and the mechanisms of disease transmission must be analyzed separately, as they have unique impacts on the spread of epidemics.

In this study, we examine a type of manifold called a three-dimensional nearly Kenmotsu manifold. By introducing a Cotton soliton, we analyze its compatibility with the structure of the manifold. Specifically, we prove that any such soliton structure cannot exist in a non-flat, three-dimensional nearly Kenmotsu manifold. Furthermore, if the soliton structure does exist, it implies that the manifold is of constant curvature. This outcome also applies to constant curvature 1-formal Sasakian Sasimantor soliton structures.

This paper outlines a framework for constructing and developing PDF fitting programs. It details the mathematical equations underlying these programs and discusses various methods for analyzing and assessing their consistency, including Monte Carlo experiments, cross-validation, and Bayesian model comparison, with references to relevant research. Additionally, the framework can serve as a guide for developing new initiatives in PDF research, including open-source tools for analysis. Notably, the author has utilized this framework to present the results of an analysis combining diverse datasets, utilizing the FWIFT fitting framework.

Off-line reinforcement learning, utilizing previously collected data, enables the swift adaptation of autonomous agents to new environments and tasks. A successful implementation depends on the autonomy agent's ability to effectively combine prior knowledge with new experiences for effective policy optimization. This success relies heavily on the situation-dependent statistical properties of the data presented to the autonomy agent. Specifically, the agent benefits from minimized data variance through effective strategy optimization techniques, including policy gradient methods. We introduce an innovative approach called variance diminution experience replay (VDER), which combines multiple statistically distinct batch datasets to create a more consistent data distribution, thereby enhancing the efficiency of policy optimization algorithms. We showcase that integrating our VDER technique with the actor-critic algorithm results in accelerated convergence and improved convergence to optimal solutions, ultimately enhancing the autonomy agent's learning capabilities.

I'd like to introduce libcommute, a versatile C++11/14/17 template library designed for manipulating quantum operator algebras, extending the functionality of the underlying domain-specific language 'pycommute'. This powerful toolset forms the foundation for the development of complex quantum systems, whereas simpler systems can be easily constructed using pycommute, libcommute enables a balance between high-level abstract manipulation and precise, low-level computer representation, thereby making it an ideal foundation for exact diagonalization processes. The features of pycommute and libcommute can be leveraged to create novel methods, such as the shell model, and facilitate integration with other algorithms, including tensor network techniques, by way of customizable import/export options, the distinctive characteristics of libcommute/pycommute make it a versatile foundation for computational quantum many-body problem research, the project's web page is available at http://commute.quanteon.org/, and the license terms can be found in the project's README, with additional details about libcommute available within the package itself, whereas pycommute can be found on PyPI under 'pycommute', on GitHub at https://github.com/libcommute/pycommute, and on Gitee at https://gitee.com/zyh86/pycommute, respectively.

Recent studies on iron-based superconductors have highlighted the presence of an electronic nematic state above the vestigial antiferromagnetic transition, suggesting an electronic symmetry breaking where translational and spin symmetries remain intact. Translational symmetry typically displays minimal effects on angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) data. In this investigation, we utilize high-resolution ARPES to examine the electronic and superconducting gaps in bulk single crystals of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$, a state that exhibits no intrinsic nematicity. Our findings reveal that the Fermi surface pockets originating from the two nickelate layers are of comparable size. Moreover, we employ a global fitting procedure to a dispersion models to the (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ data, a method often utilized while assuming the nematic state's fictional larger gaps. Our high-resolution data indicate the smaller gaps align with prior reports, whereas the larger gaps represent an interpretation of the nematic state. Nevertheless, our data suggest the larger gaps may not be necessary, a conclusion supported by a prominent neutron interference effect observed in the larger Fermi surface pocket.

Two methods for handling the nonlinear component of a vector source in the QCD partition function are examined, specifically the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization technique. A demonstration is made that these methods yield the same outcome when applying the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation to the quark partition function results in a nonlinear term inconsistent with the Bagge-Bodwin formula for the QCD vacuum energy. In contrast, superbosonization achieves the correct transformation and a direct correspondence is drawn between these two approaches.

Initial findings from a measurement of the top quark's longitudinal polarization, produced through single top quark production via the t-channel process, have been reported and corroborated by previous results from direct comparisons and a statistical combination with data taken at a second interaction point. This measurement uses an optimized reconstruction of the top quark's momentum, derived from both kinematic constraints and the decay products of the W boson, specifically utilizing the distribution of the spin analysis variable, m_T^(tqℓ). Consequently, the polarization coefficient was calculated as 0.103 ± 0.018 (statistical uncertainty ± systematic uncertainty), which aligns well with Standard Model predictions of approximately 0.11 ± 0.01.

The critical thickness transition in the la$_3$/laos bilayer system from an insulating to a metallic state has been the subject of significant scientific discussion. To determine the cause of this transition, multiple groups conducted experiments by growing la$_3$ layers of varying thickness on laos substrates. However, these previous studies did not provide enough control to distinguish between outcomes resulting from surface effects and those stemming from bulk properties. As a consequence, research using $\beta$-detected NMR with highly pure $^8$li has been able to establish the metallic nature of the la$_3$ layers while maintaining a constant, well-defined carrier concentration. These NMR findings also revealed the presence of antiferromagnetic order within these metallic la$_3$ layers at temperatures below 110 K.

In our analysis of conversational AI, we've observed a widespread simplicity that often overlooks the complexity and diversity inherent in human conversations. To address this shortcoming, we've developed "MultiTalk," a comprehensive dataset encompassing a wide array of conversation styles and genres. Specifically, "MultiTalk" features over 900,000 conversation options, spanning more than 30,000 unique contexts, and 60,000 possible responses, all of which have been approved by human inputs. We explored various aspects of the dataset, including its underlying structure, key characteristics, and initial challenges, in order to highlight the diversity inherent in human conversations. To effectively tackle the complexity, we propose the use of specialized conversation modules, each trained to handle a specific type of conversation, all of which can collaborate to overcome the challenges posed by the dataset. We believe that MultiTalk will serve as a pivotal benchmark for future models, prompting them to tackle the diversity challenge in a more holistic manner, and potentially inspire the development of comprehensive conversation agents capable of navigating the full spectrum of human interactions.

This research analyzes and calculates the average data rate for a wireless communication system, consisting of a single source and multiple destinations in a large array of antennas, is helped by a smart antenna system. Both this study and its reference are focused on measuring the average data rate in a scenario where the antennas have interrelated signals, which is common in array technology and involves a phase shift that changes over time and affects a significant portion of the antennas. By using advanced mathematical models and accounting for these factors, this study derives a formula for the average data rate, which can be used to design system components and evaluate new methods in this field. For systems with a large number of destination antennas, this study develops an efficient estimation method for the average data rate using a transformation approach, which provides a more accurate prediction than existing methods and is supported by experimental results.

We introduce an efficient computational method to simulate large collections of particles in modified gravity theories of the type $f(R)$ or RS2, which we find is comparable to running similar simulations in General Relativity. Our method involves mapping these modified gravity scenarios onto their General Relativity counterparts and utilizing the same computational codes, preserving the particle counts and distributions while only adjusting the gravitational strength. Although there are some minor differences, the large-scale structures formed in these modified gravity simulations are largely consistent with those formed in General Relativity when the gravitational coupling strengths are set to their typical values. Our code achieves an order of magnitude speed increase over standard $N$-body particle simulation codes in representing the evolution of matter within these modified gravity scenarios. Moreover, our method can also be applied to any theoretical model that differs from General Relativity.

Building on the established connection between the Gaussian free field and multiple stochastic Loewner evolutions, our work extends this relationship to a new system of randomly interacting particles. Specifically, we construct a multiple stochastic Loewner evolution driven by a one-dimensional gas of particles whose interactions are influenced by an external potential, all on the real line. From this evolution, we derive a collection of domains and subsequently define a corresponding Riemann surface. Our main achievement is demonstrating that this surface has the properties of a scalar Gaussian free field with specific boundary conditions, analogous to the case of multiple Loewner evolutions and their relationship to the uniformization of simply connected subsets of the complex plane.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source derivative that can be deployed as a media-serving platform for 'over-the-shoulder' collaboration on complex tasks involving multiple steps. WorkingWiki has been particularly useful in scenarios requiring significant coordination, such as organizing large-scale conferences. Its features have been utilized to develop conference-specific tools and facilitate the review process for accepted sessions. This project's source code and subsequent developments are openly shared on GitHub.

This study re-examines the combustion characteristics of a turbulent methane-air jet flame experiencing acoustic disturbances, using an active flame model. The model considers reactions within a flame-bracketed region, where fuel is consumed and products are formed, represented by separate diffusion equations. A new linearity assumption has been added to the model, based on a prior discovery that reaction rates in turbulent flames scale linearly with local turbulence intensity. Experimental data from a wind-tunnel experiment supported this linearity assumption. Using this, the equations were simplified to focus on mean values, enabling analysis of reaction-product interactions and their effects on turbulent flame dynamics. The results showed that acoustic fluctuations in wind speeds and temperature caused chemical product imbalances, contributing significantly to flame behavior, particularly in affecting scalar dissipation rates. The active flame model showed a better alignment with direct numerical simulation data, further validating the active flame approach within a linearized framework. The concept of an active flame model may have broader applications in understanding combustion processes in the context of flame stability, wave propagation, auto-ignition, and flame collisions.

We propose a novel concept called topological states within the context of stellar 
oscillations, linking star properties with the behavior of their pulsation modes 
through mathematics similar to topology. These internal dynamics can be described 
using a matrix and its associated spectral properties. Specifically, we show that 
stars exhibiting comparable topological descriptions possess similar spectral 
characteristics affecting the stability of their oscillation frequencies. This 
relationship enables the grouping of stellar oscillations into distinct states, 
where the precision of this classification is directly influenced by a stellar 
topological index. Furthermore, this framework is supported by simulations of 
convection processes in labs, showing that specific features in dynamics spectra 
can be related to the underlying stellar properties and affect the behavior of 
pulsation modes.

A recently discovered phenomenon, known as tripolar dynamics or traveling waves, stands in contrast to another, more widely studied one, called multistable chimera states, where some units are synchronized while others are dispersed. Both effects, previously observed only as isolated occurrences, were now now observed coexisting within the same network, representing a new discovery called a chimera multistable state. Furthermore, a newly proposed method, based on analyzing the relationship between pairs of units, was now able to accurately classify the nature of dynamics by distinguishing between different states, such as synchronized units exhibiting high correlation and disordered units exhibiting random behavior. This method was particularly effective when applied to units exhibiting similar correlation patterns.

A newly developed variant of the 2D Ising model, based on a square lattice, has been explored, based on an on-site spin variable and adjacent site cluster indicators, defined through Heaviside functions that determine the presence of particles at specific points. An extensive numerical analysis was conducted using Monte Carlo simulations across a wide parameter range, encompassing varying temperatures and Heaviside function definitions. These analyses led to significant findings where, at low temperatures and with certain Heaviside function configurations, distinct temperature thresholds were identified. Above these thresholds, the model exhibits standard critical behavior, mirroring the behavior of the conventional 2D Ising model. Conversely, below these thresholds, extreme order dominates the system, characterized by minimal entropy and no spontaneous fluctuations. Notably, specific Heaviside function definitions gave rise to exotic behavior, resulting in the discovery of a new type of cluster-based clustering phenomenon.

We have studied the impact of very low mass dark matter on neutrinoless double beta decay experiments, particularly when the masses are so small that they behave like a periodic oscillating wave, potentially interfering with the experiments' ability to distinguish between different types of decays. Given the extremely long wavelength of very low mass dark matter, we treated the problem within local flat spacetime and analyzed its effects on the decay phase space and the nuclear transition, which is essential for detecting the process. The key observation from our research indicates that the experiments will primarily measure a combination of the Standard Model parameters and the amplitude of the wave's modulation. Assuming the discovery of neutrinoless double beta decay, we have derived considerable constraints on the mass of dark matter with a focus on its influence on Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and the present-day data from the Type Ia supernovae and the expansion of the universe. Even in the most favorable circumstances, the derived constraints imply the masses of dark matter are too large for it to be the source of the universe's dark matter.

Existing models for predicting the flux of ultra-high energy cosmic ray photons are incomplete and inconsistent with recent experimental findings, especially regarding their energy spectrum and spatial distribution. New data indicate a significant component of ultra-high energy cosmic rays may originate from ultraviolet phenomena. This new component exhibits a continuous energy spectrum, in contrast to the discrete patterns of current models based on hadronic decay and photopion decay. Also, the spatial distribution of ultra-high energy cosmic ray photons remains poorly understood, largely due to uncertainties in photodisintegration thresholds for the nuclear interaction. This study introduces basic models based on hadronic decay and photopion decay processes, as well as simulation experiments to understand and compare possible methods for producing ultra-high energy cosmic ray photons. These models incorporate various interaction and decay processes, as well as the effects of solar magnetic fields and pair production. Calculations show that hadronic interaction alone is insufficient to explain ultra-high energy cosmic ray photons due to pair production within the solar magnetic field. Nevertheless, hadronic and photopion interactions, combined with pair production, can successfully account for a significant flux of ultra-high energy cosmic ray photons with energies below approximately $10$ EeV.

Nonlocal gravity theory proposes that the geometry of spacetime is directly related to a material property known as a constitutive relation between the dielectric permittivity tensor and matter. In a nonlocal theory, this relationship occurs over a scale larger than that of a single point, which protects against the loss of nonlocality during the process of simplification, or diagonalization, of the dielectric tensor. To better understand this, we model spacetime as having a frame material property and create a constitutive relation that preserves this nonlocality. This allows us to derive a nonlocal field equation and, in the process, protect a frame invariant that would otherwise become undefined. This has the potential to limit the range of possible frame transformations. In the case of a single matter field, this process can be simplified to an effective stress-energy tensor, which, for a specific transformation, becomes singular. This may provide the basis for the observed phenomena of gravitational collapse and the formation of black holes.

Conflicting writes to the same location in a replicated data structure are a common issue in modern systems that use eventual consistency models. To maintain high performance and simplicity, these systems often sacrifice strict serializability. As the number of conflicts increases, developers typically resort to repairing code, but this process can be time-consuming and painful, resulting in significant effort expenditure. We propose a new framework called Remove-Win, which is a design framework for conflict-free replicated data structures that allows users to easily specify consistency behavior, leading to initial implementation times as fast as one-fifth of traditional methods. The framework consists of a set of building blocks representing different repair strategies, a conflict analysis component that predicts operation ordering and conflict behavior, as well as a compiler and supporting tools for building conflict-free structures. The versatility of the framework is demonstrated through the development of a conflict-free set, a consistency-enhanced version of a conflict-sensitive accumulator, and a consistency-improved counter array, all of which outperform previous designs in terms of conflict handling and consistency. The framework's potential to produce well-behaved conflict-free structures is further highlighted by a comparative analysis of conflict patterns, where the repair strategies of Remove-Win outperform a previous state-of-the-art design in terms conflict performance. The framework's design and implementation are realized through the conflict-free programming language CFPL, which provides a robust foundation for the development of conflict-free structures. The framework's components, including the compiler and repair strategies, are available for public use and

Functional genomics offers a detailed understanding of how genomic elements work together to regulate gene expression and interact across the genome. Despite its potential value, fully exploring this complexity is hindered by current methods that assess only small, isolated regions. To address this challenge, researchers at the Weizmann Science Complex utilized functional data from the ENCODE project to study a smaller subset of the genome – a 2MB region – in two individuals. By combining this high-resolution map with existing genome-wide association studies for 18 different traits including height, weight, and various psychiatric conditions, they were able to identify multiple patterns of co-occurrence between functional and genetic variation associated with these traits. A newly developed statistical method was employed to evaluate the prevalence of these patterns across the human genome and was compared to random genomic sequences. The study found that certain patterns, especially those involving multiple genetic variants working in coordination with multiple functional elements, were significantly more common in regions linked to human traits than in random sequences. Notably, these enriched patterns were primarily located within the annotating elements rather than the gene coding regions. The researchers also observed a stronger association between pattern enrichment and the degree of functional element interactivity. This research highlights the significance of considering multiple forms of genomic variation and functional element relationships in understanding the complex relationship between the genome and human health.
This thesis has a focus on rare events in particle physics that occur as unintended results of primary collisions and research into them spans beyond the boundaries of this topic.

Observations of low-mass X-ray binaries in the galaxy's center reveal a diverse range of recurrence intervals between outbursts, spanning from less than a year to more than a decade.  Considerable effort has been made to understand the factors contributing to the quiescent outburst phases of these systems.  Some researchers suggest that the recurrence intervals in these systems may be linked to the accumulation of accreting matter at the surface of the neutron star.  A commonly used framework for assessing this idea involves comparing the time it takes for matter to accumulate to the time it takes for a type X X-ray burst to occur.  A more in-depth analysis of these systems' outburst phases revealed that the typical recurrence interval for a system is directly related to the difference between the neutron star's spin frequency and the frequency of quiescent X-ray flux variations.  This relationship appears to be established in the galaxy's center but is not observed in the inner planes of the galaxy.  As a result, matter accumulation is not believed to be the cause of the diverse range of outburst recurrence intervals seen in quiescent X-ray binaries within the inner planes of the galaxy.  Instead, proposed alternatives to the matter accumulation theory include theories suggesting that the diverse range of outburst recurrence intervals may be linked to the amount of matter being accumulated or the amount of heat being retained within the accretion disk.

The dynamics of a particular class of celestial bodies, characterized by a wide separation between their component stars, can no longer be accurately modeled using Newtonian gravity alone. This is particularly true when considering the component stars as point masses. Observations of these celestial bodies, often referred to as "wide binaries," have the potential to test the limitations of Newtonian gravity and may suggest a more accurate model that takes into account the finite size of the stars. This more accurate model could also help to explain the observed behavior of pulsars within a wide binary system, without requiring a dark companion for one of the components. Consideration must also be given to the stars' radius in determining the stable orbital distances of these wide binaries. A particular formula, derived within a post-Newtonian framework, offers predictions for these stable orbital distances that closely align with those observed in a Monte Carlo simulation. This prediction holds true even when applying a standard two-body model. Furthermore, the accurate modeling of the wide binary system reveals additional insights into the detection of exoplanets orbiting the component stars. This detection method, referred to as the "astrometric method," has a greater detection range than previously estimated, approximately doubling it, because wide binaries with short orbital periods can still support the stable detection of wide-planets through this method.

Radio sources known as compact faint (CO) sources are extensively used in galaxy formation research, but their precise properties remain unclear due to limitations imposed by radio sensitivity and resolution. To address this, researchers created stacked spectra and images of CO sources categorized by angular size. They analyzed two distinct samples of CO sources linked to infrared galaxies and active galactic nuclei across six frequency bands from 48 MHz to 1.4 GHz. By examining the spectral properties of these sources, they discovered that CO sources with a size less than 3 arcseconds exhibit a flatter spectrum than those between 3-10 arcseconds, which in turn are more turbulent than the CO sources less than 3 arcseconds. Additionally, CO sources between 3-10 arcseconds exhibit more turbulent characteristics than those between 10-30 arcseconds.

This research analyzes the impact of one-dimensional wave bursts exiting a star during its explosion. These bursts can occur due to a sudden closure of a safety valve, as seen in jets exiting a main star or a pair of colliding stars. To understand the effect of these bursts on the escaping material, various scenarios were modeled using conservative hydrodynamics. The results indicate that in most cases, the star's explosion will eventually produce a shock wave that moves faster than the speed of sound. However, one specific scenario required a more in-depth analysis to reach this conclusion. Additionally, the speed at which this shock wave moves is heavily influenced by the speed of the burst and the amount of material it encounters.

This brief work extends a previously discovered connection between algebraic weights and mathematical weights, building on past research. We incorporate this expansion into the framework of non-mathematical weights introduced in associated documentation.

Connections between atoms and their surrounding environment, particularly lattice vibrations, have significant value for studying a wide range of materials and physical phenomena. However, current experimental and theoretical methods for analyzing these interactions are limited to static measurements based on average values, incapable of capturing dynamic processes influenced by the atoms' motion through space. By formulating a theoretical framework that accounts for the material's movement, we can examine a wide range of new effects arising from dynamic interactions, such as electron acceleration and aerodynamic drag on phonons. Consequently, this novel theoretical perspective enables the prediction of significant, previously unexplained phenomena, including asymmetric electron distributions, non-reciprocal material properties, and electromagnetic wave rectification.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a significant area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These lecture notes have been compiled with material presented over various seminars in the past two years and will provide a clear and user-friendly introduction to the fundamental aspects of $\tau$-tilting theory, along with several key results. Additionally, it will explore several recent major development within the field.

The impressive capabilities of modern neural models in generating human-like text have prompted the creation of dialogue datasets tailored for evaluating and advancing their performance. Nonetheless, a critical shortcoming of a popular evaluation benchmark, Natural Language inference for Dialogue (NLFD), is its allowance of only two semantic variants of text within the same dialogue. This limitation hinders a more accurate assessment and improvement of models' comprehension of multi-turn conversations. In response, we introduce a new, expanded version of the NLFD benchmark, featuring at least six distinct semantic variants per dialogue, thereby enabling a nuanced evaluation of models' semantic diversity in natural conversation.

Automated driving systems depend on predicting the dangers surrounding a vehicle, necessitating the development of a reliable and efficient method for identifying hazardous actions.  A dataset of 382 video clips from real-world drivers was assembled and a baseline model based on spatial-temporal segmentation mask transfer was established to assess the difficulty of detecting dangerous behavior.  A significant performance improvement of nearly 10% was achieved with the new model, which utilizes full-frame extraction for temporal dimension analysis and partial-frame transfer for mask transfer.  A comparison with other prominent approaches further validated the model's reliability and confirmed that it offers superior performance.

The potential for precise fundamental frequency pattern identification in rotating low-mass celestial bodies has been highlighted by recent discovery of the first known, rapidly spinning brown dwarf, J1407-B99. This breakthrough underscores the value of continued time-domain astrophysical spectroscopic project - brown dwarf initiative observations in establishing a comprehensive, rotating substellar object spectrum. To support this endeavor, we developed a comprehensive, rotating substellar object simulation model that incorporates general relativity, thermal physics, equation of state, surface processes, and mass conservation in a rotating frame of reference. Our simulations span the full mass-shedding limit spectrum across diverse object parameters, yielding accurate fundamental frequency predictions that match observed data within one sigma margin of error. Notably, this research reveals that higher-spinning objects exhibit thinner atmospheric layers, reducing the likelihood of mode identification due to suppressed temperature variations. Additionally, accurate mode interpretation demands consideration of relativistic effects and spin-induced shape alterations.

In complex particle physics experiments, especially those involving hadron production and the subsequent analysis of final hadrons, amplitude analyses are highly effective in determining the spins and decay paths of transient resonances. However, their success relies on accurately modeling various experimental influences, such as detection efficiencies and mass biases, which can affect the data in resonance regions. Often, the same modeling approaches are used to simulate the experimental setup and the data analysis, leading to seemingly minor discrepancies with actual measurements. In this study, we explore the consequences of these discrepancies on amplitude analyses and propose a method to independently model the effects on the data. By comparing our approach to the traditional method and running a full simulation of the LHCb  Geant4 experimental setup for $Lb^+ \to (K^+X), $ we demonstrate that our proposed method better matches the data and provides a more precise description of the resonant $K^+X$ system.

A particular outcome in the density wind afterglow model is inconsistent with observations of afterglows associated with both Gamma-ray bursts and supernovae. This discrepancy highlights a fundamental understanding gap in the realm of cosmological gamma-ray bursts, gamma-ray sources, and afterglows. In contrast, a dynamic progression of fireballs, influenced by their surrounding media, can now be depicted through a new, universally applicable model. This novel model can resolve multiple issues related to gamma-ray bursts, including the density wind afterglow discrepancy, through a series of equations describing the evolution of gamma-ray burst fluxes based on fireball energy and media density. By doing so, it becomes possible to predict afterglow behavior and place objects on a trajectory that reflects their surrounding media's density. A new, previously unobserved class of gamma-ray bursts, known as "Carlyle-Afterglows," can now be defined using a new threshold, and the existence of fast radio bursts can also be explained through "Matched-GRB/Afterglow" interactions.

A bipartite graph can be formed from any two sets of elements, X and Y, where an edge connects a unique pair of elements from X and Y. A mapping then splits X into two new subsets, maintaining the bipartite nature of the graph. A bipartite vertex splitting problem arises when seeking the smallest possible subset of X, such that after removing it, X becomes two disjoint subsets that result in two separate bipartite graphs. We have developed a new approach for calculating this problem in relation to a fixed number k of edges. Specifically, our algorithm runs in O(2^(4k)^3 * (k!)* (k^2)* n^3 ) time for a graph with n vertices.

Deep neural network-based image classification models have been widely used in recent years, but their practical application is limited due to high costs and varying performance across different scenarios. Continual learning has emerged as an effective approach to address this issue, allowing models to adapt to new classes and environments. However, most incremental learning scenarios involve adding new classes, where existing models suffer from performance declines and increased errors. In this paper, a comprehensive comparative study of diverse incremental learning methods for the insertion of new classes is conducted. We evaluate the effectiveness of various methods in terms of their ability to handle class imbalance in these scenarios. Ultimately, we highlight the most successful strategy and demonstrate its superiority in outperforming other approaches.

This paper describes a novel method for optimizing the efficiency of bipedal robots walking without relying on a self-correcting gait cycle. We propose using thrusters to minimize fall probability as an alternative approach to reducing collision probability, which is a common focus in current research. Based on this alternative approach, we developed an evaluation method involving random sampling to assess the stability of various gait designs. To efficiently evaluate a wide range of parameters in the design space, we created a highly efficient algorithm to generate thruster-assisted 3TIP walks for a two-link robot. Our results demonstrate that the added complexity of implementing this approach is justified by significant improvements in orbital stability and robustness, particularly for walks with a limited number of degrees of freedom. Furthermore, our method exhibits greater robustness than traditionally optimized walks, even those achieved through random sampling, and can withstand substantial perturbations, including impacts equivalent to 15 times the robot's weight, without failing.

Let $A$ be a local domain with an associated maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$. This work explores conditions for $A$ to have a total residue map, where every element in the fraction field $K$ can be expressed as $xc + x'$, with $c$ being an element of $A$, $x$ belonging to the maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$, and $x'$ in $A$. Total residue maps are connected to Japanese properties for domains, specifically valuation rings and Hilbert's 14th problem. We provide a valuation-theoretic explanation for Okubo's finding that local domains with a total residue map possess a specific multiplicity property, and we show that domains with a total residue map are nearly valuations, sharing some finite-dimensional characteristic with valuations.

In response to the diminishing cost-effectiveness of pushing for higher MIPS on modern CPUs, a counterintuitive approach emerges by leveraging frequency reduction to improve both energy efficiency and latency in MIPS calculations within typical application scenarios. A comprehensive framework, HyperDegrade, is proposed as it systematically explores the benefits of operating modern x86 CPUs at lower frequencies, outperforming alternative energy-efficient methods based on benchmark evaluations conducted using diverse workloads running HyperDegrade at various frequency levels. HyperDegrade's hidden dimensionality is addressed via automated search for optimal frequency configurations, demonstrated through implementations utilizing system-wide frequency control and programmable memory compilers, respectively. The evaluations indicate that operating at approximately 1/10th of a CPU's peak frequency, or utilizing HyperCompile, can yield up to 1.5x to 2.5x extensions in energy-efficient performance, as supported by extensive benchmarks utilizing applications ranging from web servers to media players and machine learning workflows.

We investigate a potential new contribution to the hadronic vacuum polarization anomaly from the interaction of two photons, involving a novel two-loop diagram with the Higgs boson. Although the Standard Model has a negligible effect due to a small coupling of the photon to the Higgs, various beyond Standard Model scenarios can produce a measurable impact, as they propose new particles or modified interactions not present in the Standard Model. Given its role in electroweak symmetry breaking, adding the S-channel contribution from the Higgs boson is a logical extension to any model proposing a new scalar or vector particle. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a new, complex-interacting Higgs boson can have a significant effect on the hadronic vacuum polarization anomaly, thus providing an intriguing possibility for the anomaly's source to be rooted in Standard Model with however its importance should not surpass models proposing novel physics beyond the Standard Model.

Using LHCb data from 2015 and 2016 at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, phasing is measured from $B_{\gamma\gamma}$ decays where neutral $B$ mesons decay into charged $K^+\pi^-$ for both $B^0$ and $B^+$ particles. L0 reconstruction of these decays yields direct CP violation values of $6.9\% \pm 1.4\% \pm 0.4\%$ for $B^0$ and $4.7\% \pm 1.3\% \pm 0.3\%$ for $B^0$, consistent with previous measurements. Additionally, radiative decays into $K^0_{\rm S}\pi^0$ provide a way to measure CP violation without relying on $K^0_{\rm S}$ decay vertex fitting. By regenerating the $K^0_{\rm S}$ decay point from $K^0_{\rm S}\to K^+K^-$ decay products, an impact parameter is formed. The CP-odd and CP-even components of $B^0\to K^0_{\rm S} \pi^0$ decays exhibit distinct transverse directions of this impact parameter, and the asymmetry in the direction of d0 between conjugate decay modes measures direct CP violation. A disentangling node has been proposed as a new element in welded virtual knot theory, featuring a specific disentanglement connection between two knots. This concept effectively addresses the limitations of classical and multi-variable invariants in assessing disentangled knots. A new invariant function has been devised for welded virtual knots that include disentangling nodes, and its validity has been confirmed through an extensive examination of the nine-component link diagram set. A fundamental operation rule for disentangling nodes has also been established and applied to derive an easier calculation method for the invariant function. This method has been利用 to distinguish various complex configurations, such as the Melmed link, Borromean ring, and other multi-component link sets. A connection has furthermore been found between disentangling nodes and crossing changes, allowing for an easier determination of disjointness between virtual knot components.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve $\Gamma$ has a finite set of generators, $\Sigma$, over the tropical semifield $k\langle t\rangle$. The result provides a path to establishing the rational function semifield as a finitely presented $k\langle t\rangle$-semialgebra. Furthermore, if the tropical curve is defined by a polynomial equation, we determine the number of generators required, equal to the rank of its associated divisor group.

We've demonstrated that I^3 involves comparing the linking numbers of two specific spaces, the standard torus T^2 in R^3 and the Fox-Hatcher loop formed by connecting three non-minimal arcs within it. This finding enables a volume formula for tensor products of knot types to be derived, building on a result by Shiraev which relates matrix coefficients of the Kuperberg invariant and an explicit basis for long knots.

New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides strong evidence against a previously reported exception to the combined conservation of energy and momentum in a well-controlled experiment involving beta decay of molecular tritium.  If this finding is correct, the minimum possible value for at least one neutrino mass must be greater than or equal to 1.1 times 10 to the power of -4 eV.  Assuming the three lightest neutrino masses meet the established minimum value, a lower bound is placed on the sum of the three neutrino masses derived from oscillation data, specifically stating that this sum is greater than or equal to 1.29 times 10 to the power of -4 eV.  Given current cosmological constraints, it is highly probable that the three lightest neutrino masses adopt their minimum possible value.  As a result, if the minimum possible value for at least one neutrino mass is greater than or equal to 1.1 times 10 to the power of -4 eV, the ratio of the second to first largest neutrino mass ratios (either the medium-to-heavy or light-to-medium ratio) is highly probable that it will be greater than or equal to 0.9.  Researcher(s) utilize existing and recently published data from various laboratory and cosmological experiments to establish such lower bounds, making their study's conclusions directly relevant to the ongoing KATRIN experiment's efforts to provide more precise upper bounds for neutrino mass

This paper examines and compares the sequential (CPU) and parallel (GPU) approaches to matrix multiplication, presenting (a) the code for CPU matrix multiplication using basic for-loops, as well as an optimized version employing 2D arrays and row-major ordering, and (b) the code for parallel matrix multiplication employing a CUDA approach. As a result, this study yields the following outcomes: (a) basic for-loop Loops yield a performance of approximately 20 operations per second, while optimized 2D arrays Loops achieve a performance of approximately 200 operations per second, and (b) parallel matrix multiplication using GPU technology can accomplish the same task in about 0.05 seconds.

In many real-world applications, it is crucial to synchronize a group of agents within a network to perform tasks simultaneously. To achieve this, we propose a new approach called Strategic Multi-Task Synchronization (SMTS), which ensures that agents cooperate to schedule and execute tasks at the same time. This method takes into account the self-interested nature of agents who may aim to optimize their individual schedules and minimize their execution costs. By representing this scenario as a game, we provide conditions for its convergence to an equilibrium state and a method to provide incentives through payment schemes to promote cooperative behavior and synchronize the group of agents within a network.

We utilize the amplitude-based resummation technique to compute the effective shift in the $\pi$ decay rate caused by infrared effects at the next-to-leading order. The calculation shows that using a well-defined mass scheme can recover the naive expected total decay rate for effective charges below a specific threshold. The outcome can be accurately modeled by incorporating an effective charge that takes into account the impact of infrared loops on virtual photon exchange. Introducing a suitable cutoff in phase space can prevent unphysically enhanced higher-order corrections in the comparison. Intended for a broader scientific audience, this demonstration of the method is accompanied by additional discussions on the topic. Introducing suitable screening effects in an extended QED model for a charged scalar can have an unexpected outcome, namely, the effective charge appearing in the loop can lead to an enhanced $\pi$ decay rate, which contradicts the initial expectation.
